This week, I saw a master of processes in action. Everything was optimized, and at the same time, the customer experience was excellent. Whom am I talking about? 👓 My ophthalmologist. You make the appointment online and get a reminder message one week and one day before (this is standard for French online platforms). When you arrive, the secretariat is next to the entry, so a search is unnecessary. At this stage, there are no medical papers. Then, there is the waiting room just next to it. You enter and sit down. Then the doctor comes, and it gives you complete attention, from the invite to the cabinet to the end. He only takes your name and has the history on his screen (one screen, no clicking). The doctor asks for any changes or problems, does an examination, and always gives you full attention. He answers questions you might have. Then he guides you to the secretary who handles all the paperwork, including the payment. The visit is short, but I do not find it a disadvantage. The doctor does what he does best, and only that. The rest of the team handles the paperwork, schedule, and everything else. 🔥 What if all specialists (medical and everyone else) organized their work this way? Do you do things you excel in, or also "stuff"? PS. I'm not giving the doctor's name because he'll be retiring soon and is not taking any new patients. My Berkeley College students and I designed our own AI policy together. This is how we approached it. (I'll include the basic policy at the end of this post) 1. We talked about what they already knew. → We started in teams and shared. → Then, we talked together. 2. We used ChatGPT. → Quite a few students never used it before. → Several students had no idea what this was. → We talked about what was happening. 3. We used Claude. → I wanted to move away from ChatGPT. → I showed them how it could create games. 4. We used Google'S NotebookLM. → I wanted to talk more about multimodal AI. → My students were thoroughly unimpressed. → We talked about voice clones (the good and the bad) 5. We talked about AI-generated images. → We did this with Dall-E, through ChatGPT. 6. We played Leon Furze 's Real vs. Fake Game → Students had to pick out AI-generated images. → They did well, and got 7/10. → We talked about AI and misinformation. 7. We brainstormed about benefits and risks. → We talked about using AI for brainstorming and for getting past the blank page. → We talked about the loss of voice, the unethical practices used in training, the impact on the environment. If students had a question, I answered it to the best of my knowledge. We were as holistic as possible. ----------------------- Then, we created a policy. Here is what my students wanted. 1️⃣ Full Transparency → They'll tell me when and how they use it. → I'll tell them when I use it. 2️⃣ AI Scale → They thought Leon Furze 's scale was fair. → Parts of an assignment get a number from 1-5. → 1 = No AI → 5 = Full-On AI → Most activities will be in the middle. 3️⃣ AI is to be used carefully and only for specific purposes that help us learn. → It is not to be used lightly. → It hurts our environment and can hurt our voices. → We need to use it carefully or not at all. → We can use it for brainstorming, outlining, and feedback. → But we are not allowed to use it to write. That would be unfair and defeat the purpose of the course. So, that's it. That will be their policy. It was student-created, by students working out in the open and collaboratively. …more

Have you heard of the term hashtag # AITransformation ? AI transformation refers to the process of integrating artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into various aspects of an organization to drive significant change in operations, decision-making, products, services, and overall business strategy. It goes beyond adopting AI tools and involves a comprehensive overhaul of business processes, culture, and mindset to fully leverage AI’s capabilities for innovation and efficiency. AI transformation is a subset of hashtag # DigitalTransformation , but with a specific focus on utilizing AI-driven insights, automation, and intelligence to create value. Key Components of AI Transformation: Strategic AI Integration AI transformation requires embedding AI into the core business strategy, aligning AI applications with organizational goals such as improving customer experience, optimizing operations, or developing new revenue streams. Data-Driven Decision Making AI transformation emphasizes the use of advanced data analytics, machine learning, and predictive models to drive more informed and faster decision-making. Organizations must build robust data infrastructures to support AI models. Process Automation AI transformation often involves automating repetitive, time-consuming tasks through AI-powered tools, such as robotic process automation (RPA), natural language processing (NLP), or intelligent chatbots, thereby improving efficiency and reducing costs. Enhanced Customer Experience AI enables organizations to offer personalized, real-time services through tools like recommendation systems, sentiment analysis, and predictive customer support, improving engagement and satisfaction. Innovation in Products and Services AI transformation allows companies to create new AI-enabled products and services, such as AI-driven health diagnostics, autonomous vehicles, or intelligent financial advisory systems, which can open up new markets and revenue streams. Workforce Evolution Successful AI transformation includes upskilling the workforce to work alongside AI. Employees need training on how to interact with AI tools, interpret AI-generated insights, and manage AI-driven processes. AI Ethics and Governance As AI becomes more integral to business functions, organizations must establish clear ethical guidelines, data privacy standards, and governance frameworks to ensure AI is used responsibly and transparently. In summary, AI transformation is a comprehensive effort to harness the power of artificial intelligence to transform the way businesses operate, make decisions, and interact with their customers, often leading to new levels of efficiency, innovation, and competitive advantage. AI-generated podcasts in education: Why they might not be the best idea Quite a few people seem to be intrigued by the idea of AI-generated podcasts made with Google NotebookLM. I get the fascination, but there are a couple of problems here: 1-- Quantity over quality: Sure, AI can help generate more podcasts than ever before. But why on Earth would we want more podcasts? I'd prefer fewer, but better ones. 2-- Copyright issues: How does this technology address ethical concerns, bias, and copyrighted material? There's still a very real risk of intellectual property infringement here. 3-- Redundant curation: While generative AI is great at summarizing unstructured content across vast amounts of information, using it to generate educational podcasts seems misguided to me. Why? Well, I believe most authors within the realm of education will tell you that textbooks already represent carefully curated content. It’s pretty much in the right, condensed form already. Summary "services" like Blinkist and Shortform have been around for a while. Perhaps the 'make your own textbook-based podcast' is a natural extension of this approach to (not) reading. Learning can take many forms besides reading books, of course, but not allowing for friction to get anywhere near your learning space seems to be a tendency. Considering that future generations will likely need to excel in critical thinking, analytical competencies, and reflection skills, this is probably not the best way forward for education. Ask yourself this: If educators were setting the agenda here instead of big tech, would AI-generated podcasts really be the first thing we would want for future learners? 🤔 …more

Instead of "a beautiful landscape," try "a sunset over a tranquil lake surrounded by snow-capped mountains, with wildflowers in the foreground." 2. Specify the Art Style: Whether you want a photorealistic image, a watercolor painting, or an anime-style drawing, clearly state the desired art style at the beginning of your prompt. For example, "Photorealistic portrait of a young woman at a bustling street fair." 4. Use Reference Images: If possible, provide reference images or describe elements from existing artworks. This helps the AI understand the style and composition you’re aiming for. 5. Experiment with Length and Structure: Sometimes a short, concise prompt works best, while other times a longer, more detailed description is needed. Experiment to see what yields the best results for your specific needs. 6. Incorporate Emotions and Adjectives: Adding emotional descriptors can enhance the depth and feel of the image. For example, "a serene, misty morning in a dense forest with soft sunlight filtering through the trees." 7. Iterate and Refine: Don’t be afraid to tweak and refine your prompts. GenAI misinformation & labelling. A cybersecurity issue or an online safety issue? This was the question I asked myself when I saw China's new draft measures for labelling GenAI content (released on 14 September; open to consultation by 13 November) 🇨🇳 The Measures cover the GenAI value chain, namely: ▪ "AI Content Generator Service Providers" must add "explicit labels" (e.g. watermarks, symbols) or "implicit labels" (e.g. metadata) to genAI content, where required. ▪ Internet Platform Operators must review and check that any uploaded content to their platforms includes genAI content. If so, they must notify the user and apply implicit labels to the content before distribution. ▪ Users must, whenever uploading genAI content to internet platforms, disclose that the content is AI-generated with appropriate labels. Non-compliance may result in liability/penalties under China's existing cybersecurity, data security, personal data protection and genAI laws. 💡 MY THOUGHTS Only the Chinese version is available (attached below). But even if you can't read Chinese (and just follow the diagrams), you'll notice some interesting/clever ideas that we could all learn: 1️⃣ While the labelling methods are not new, I found the diagrams to be so helpful. From page 12, you'll see various explicit labelling techniques such as in-line notes, footnotes, superscripts, highlighted soundwaves, corner tags, robot logos, etc. From page 20, there's instructive examples of data schemas (e.g. JSON text) for the implicit labels. Even if this draft doesn't become law for whatever reason, this document alone is already a handy reference re genAI transparency. 2️⃣ While labels are not a foolproof solution, the fact that the Measures cover the whole genAI ecosystem creates a 'web' of obligations between service providers, internet platform operators and users *at the same time* which in turn strengthens the compliance effect of labels (rather than just relying on individual self-regulation). This is different to what we're seeing in UK/US/Australia/Singapore/Korea where the relevant law mainly targets one stakeholder at a time. 3️⃣ From the title on cover page, you'll notice that this is a "cybersecurity" issue. It's an interesting contrast to the West which tend to frame genAI misinformation, deepfakes, labelling, etc as matters of "online safety". To me, cybersecurity has a stronger gravitas than online safety, and more likely to invoke a whole-of-economy response (than just social media regulation). That said, one could argue "网络安全" actually means network/online safety (not cybersecurity). Google is shaking things up with how search results look when both AI Overviews and various types of ads are included! This is especially true on mobile, where AIOs and ads appear together less often but feature more diverse ad combinations. You’ll see shopping ads and text ads placed above and below AI snippets, and sometimes even product cards within the AI-generated content. These ads stand out, pushing organic results further down the page, making it harder for them to attract traffic in mobile searches. In many cases, users might not even reach the organic results. In SE Ranking latest research on AIOs, we took a closer look at the ad landscape. Here are some key insights we discovered: → While AIOs tend to show up for informational rather than commercial keywords, we saw a lot of ads in certain niches. For example, categories like Pets, Fashion and Beauty—areas tied to e-commerce—where user queries often signal purchase intent. During our research, we noticed product cards sometimes appear within the AIOs themselves. They aren’t marked as ads yet, but they could be in the future. It’s hard to predict if Google will monetize this space, but even if they don’t, it’s smart for e-commerce brands to optimize their products on big marketplaces like Amazon or eBay, which are frequently included in AIOs. → At the moment, only a small percentage of AIOs include ads on desktop SERPs—87% of AIOs don’t show ads at all. That said, the number of ads has increased compared to last month. We’ll see how this develops as Black Friday approaches! For businesses that rely on paid ads, AIO-free SERPs are a clear advantage since it makes their ads more prominent. However, as AI Overviews roll out more widely, they’ll start appearing in more searches. Even then, ads remain effective because they often appear above the AI-generated content. Since AIOs typically show up for long-tail keywords, we’re seeing high ad visibility for those keywords, which could lead to a further decline in organic click-through rates. On the flip side, this could boost CTR for ads. I’d even guess that AIOs could influence behaviour patterns for these queries, improving overall performance for advertisers targeting these keywords. This is bound to have an impact on those whose strategies revolve around low-volume keywords. …more

California is keeping us on our toes this week with not 1 or even 2, but ~8~ new Gen AI laws signed by Gov Newsom. These laws cover a range of issues related to generative AI: transparency, rights of actors/performers regarding use of their NIL, criminalizes deepfake unauthorized sexually explicit content, and use of deepfakes in elections to misinform. SB 942 – California AI Transparency Act (Signed 9/19) Requires widely-used generative AI systems to include provenance disclosures in the content they generate. SB 926 – Amends Section 647 of the Penal Code (Signed 9/19) Creates a new crime targeting AI-generated sexually explicit deepfake content. SB 981 – An act to add Chapter 22.7 (commencing with Section 22670) to Division 8 of the Business and Professions Code, relating to social media platforms (Signed 9/19) Requires social media platforms to establish a mechanism for users to report sexually explicit deepfakes of themselves. AB 1836 – An act to amend Section 3344.1 of the Civil Code, relating to intellectual property (Signed 9/17) Prohibits commercial use of digital replicas of deceased performers in films, TV shows, video games, audiobooks, sound recordings and more, without first obtaining the consent of those performers’ estates. AB 2602 - An act to add Section 927 to the Labor Code, relating to employment (Signed 9/17) Requires contracts to specify the use of AI-generated digital replicas of a performer’s voice or likeness, and the performer must be professionally represented in negotiating the contract. Very good paper from the NATO Strategic Communications Centre of Excellence showcasing the use of AI models for targeted persuasion campaigns on social media. The paper is split in interconnected 2 parts: 1) Research focusing on real use cases of AI-Generated persuasion campaigns in the German and Russian languages (AI-generated text in less common languages has been more difficult to detect by current AI detection tools). The use cases include politically oriented content in German, pro-Kremlin messages, conspiracy theories aiming to cause unrest, and disinformation. 2) (most interesting!) A red team experiment that looks into an adversary’s potential decision making when it comes to crafting, coordinating and launching a precision persuasion campaign. The researchers used AI models to: 🔹 Define the "right" target profiles based on topics of interest. 🔹 Identify their demonstrated sentiment & behavioral tendencies (based on a clustered analysis of their posts) on those topics of interest. 🔹 Perform psychometric, behavioral, and opinion-based analysis in order to segment those social media accounts into different groups. The goal of this segmentation was to dig deeper into discovering certain traits about users that would be used in tailoring the targeting content in accordance with those psychometric characteristics. 🔹 Frame and phrase the message (the content) based on the user profile and the analysis performed in the previous steps, with the help of generative AI. The results of the output - the "tailored" messages - are very interesting. Keep in mind that this is the reality that we will be called to face in the near future. A higher scale of well-tailored information & influence campaigns that will not only come accross our own social media profiles, but also the ones of everyday people that may NOT possess the level of awareness that you potentially do, but still have a vote to cast on important topics. In any case, this is a highly recommended read. The annex includes some of the prompts along with other interesting details. CC and AI Ever since I first discovered Creative Commons during my formative years at McGill University – Faculty of Law , I’ve been captured by its simplicity and massive impact. Like the Wikimedia Foundation , the organization behind Wikipedia, the Free Encyclopedia , Creative Commons has had a massively outsized and positive effect on human knowledge and particularly creativity and intellectual property. I want to highlight Creative Commons’ recent work on artificial intelligence for creators. It charts a potential path forward that protects creators while balancing their rights with the benefits of using creative content for AI training. In the words of CC: “For over two decades we have stewarded the legal infrastructure that enables open sharing on the web. We now have an opportunity to reimagine sharing and creativity in this new age. It is time to build new infrastructure that supports better sharing with generative AI.” [...] “Generative AI presents an amazing opportunity to be a transformative tool that supports creators — both individuals and organizations — provides new avenues for creation, facilitates better sharing, enables more people to become creators, and benefits the commons of knowledge, information, and creativity for all. But there are serious concerns, such as issues around author recognition and fair compensation for creators (and the labor market for artistic work in general), the potential flood of AI-generated works on the commons making it difficult to find relevant and trustworthy information, and the disempowering effect of the privatization and enclosure of AI services and outputs, to name a few. For many creators, these and other issues may be a reason not to share their works at all under any terms, not just via CC licensing. CC wants AI to augment and support commons, not detract from it, and we want to see solutions to these concerns to avoid AI turning creators away from contributing to the commons altogether.” CC’s most recent work on GenAI has proposed the idea of Preference Sharing: “In these uncertain times, one thing is clear: there is an urgent need to develop new, nuanced approaches to digital sharing. This is Creative Commons’ speciality and we’re ready to take on this challenge by exploring a possible intervention in the AI space: preference signals.” See also their “seven principles for regulating generative AI models in order to protect the interests of creators, people building on the commons (including through AI), and society’s interests in the sustainability of the commons” linked in the comments. Neither option is ideal. This dynamic creates a real problem. Juniors are leaning heavily on AI to produce more code, but they're not developing the deeper skills needed to advance into senior roles. Meanwhile, there aren’t enough senior engineers to handle the increased volume of code. This mismatch not only affects workflow dynamics but stalls the professional growth of junior engineers. We're looking at the rise of two distinct groups: AI Code Producers: Juniors who stay stuck as juniors because they rely on AI for most of their work and miss out on the experiences that build deeper expertise. True Seniors: A shrinking group of engineers who can review and guide the AI-generated code safely into production for the long term. So no, AI isn’t replacing software engineers. California is keeping us on our toes this week with not 1 or even 2, but ~8~ new Gen AI laws signed by Gov Newsom. These laws cover a range of issues related to generative AI: transparency, rights of actors/performers regarding use of their NIL, criminalizes deepfake unauthorized sexually explicit content, and use of deepfakes in elections to misinform. SB 942 – California AI Transparency Act (Signed 9/19) Requires widely-used generative AI systems to include provenance disclosures in the content they generate. SB 926 – Amends Section 647 of the Penal Code (Signed 9/19) Creates a new crime targeting AI-generated sexually explicit deepfake content. SB 981 – An act to add Chapter 22.7 (commencing with Section 22670) to Division 8 of the Business and Professions Code, relating to social media platforms (Signed 9/19) Requires social media platforms to establish a mechanism for users to report sexually explicit deepfakes of themselves. AB 1836 – An act to amend Section 3344.1 of the Civil Code, relating to intellectual property (Signed 9/17) Prohibits commercial use of digital replicas of deceased performers in films, TV shows, video games, audiobooks, sound recordings and more, without first obtaining the consent of those performers’ estates. AB 2602 - An act to add Section 927 to the Labor Code, relating to employment (Signed 9/17) Requires contracts to specify the use of AI-generated digital replicas of a performer’s voice or likeness, and the performer must be professionally represented in negotiating the contract. AB 2655 – Defending Democracy from Deepfake Deception Act of 2024 (Signed 9/17) Requires large online platforms to remove or label deceptive and digitally altered or created content related to elections during specified periods, and requires them to provide mechanisms to report such content. AB 2839 – An act to amend Section 35 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and to add Section 20012 to the Elections Code, relating to elections, and declaring the urgency thereof, to take effect immediately (Signed 9/17) Expands the timeframe in which a committee or other entity is prohibited from knowingly distributing an advertisement or other election material containing deceptive AI-generated or manipulated content. AB 2355 – An act to amend Sections 84504, 84504.1, 84504.2, 84504.3, 84054.4, and 84504.5 of, and to add Section 84514 to, the Government Code, relating to the Political Reform Act of 1974 (Signed 9/17) Requires that electoral advertisements using AI-generated or substantially altered content feature a disclosure that the material has been altered. September 19, 2024. The day AI 🤖 made me cry. Even so, reading a summary of what I wrote for the first time was a bizarre experience, to say the least. I wasn't quite ready for the next feature... NotebookLM generated a podcast conversation between two hosts (in English?!) about my short story. Two strangers discussing the plot and expressing their (artificial) feelings towards the characters using their own (synthetic) voices. Quite surreal. So here it is. The first two minutes of this AI-generated podcast. I cut the end since it spoils everything. Naturally, this opens up many other possibilities, like creating an AI-generated video based on the same story, or producing its audio version using Text-to-Speech tools, cloning my voice, or creating a synthetic narrator's voice. My Berkeley College students and I designed our own AI policy together. This is how we approached it. (I'll include the basic policy at the end of this post) 1. We talked about what they already knew. → We started in teams and shared. → Then, we talked together. 2. We used ChatGPT. → Quite a few students never used it before. → Several students had no idea what this was. → We talked about what was happening. 3. We used Claude. → I wanted to move away from ChatGPT. → I showed them how it could create games. 4. We used Google'S NotebookLM. → I wanted to talk more about multimodal AI. → My students were thoroughly unimpressed. → We talked about voice clones (the good and the bad) 5. We talked about AI-generated images. → We did this with Dall-E, through ChatGPT. 6. We played Leon Furze 's Real vs. Fake Game → Students had to pick out AI-generated images. → They did well, and got 7/10. → We talked about AI and misinformation. 7. We brainstormed about benefits and risks. → We talked about using AI for brainstorming and for getting past the blank page. → We talked about the loss of voice, the unethical practices used in training, the impact on the environment. If students had a question, I answered it to the best of my knowledge. We were as holistic as possible. ----------------------- Then, we created a policy. Here is what my students wanted. 1️⃣ Full Transparency → They'll tell me when and how they use it. → I'll tell them when I use it. 2️⃣ AI Scale → They thought Leon Furze 's scale was fair. → Parts of an assignment get a number from 1-5. → 1 = No AI → 5 = Full-On AI → Most activities will be in the middle. 3️⃣ AI is to be used carefully and only for specific purposes that help us learn. → It is not to be used lightly. → It hurts our environment and can hurt our voices. → We need to use it carefully or not at all. → We can use it for brainstorming, outlining, and feedback. → But we are not allowed to use it to write. That would be unfair and defeat the purpose of the course. So, that's it. That will be their policy. It was student-created, by students working out in the open and collaboratively. …more

Mastering AI Image Generation: Top Prompt Engineering Tricks! Creating stunning AI-generated images is an art form in itself. With the right prompt engineering techniques, you can guide AI to produce visuals that perfectly match your vision. Here are some tips to help you craft the perfect prompts: 1. Be Specific and Descriptive: The more details you provide, the better the AI can understand your vision. Instead of "a beautiful landscape," try "a sunset over a tranquil lake surrounded by snow-capped mountains, with wildflowers in the foreground." 2. Front-Load Key Information: Start your prompt with the most important details. AI models often prioritize the beginning of the prompt, so make sure to include crucial elements early on. 3. Specify the Art Style: Whether you want a photorealistic image, a watercolor painting, or an anime-style drawing, clearly state the desired art style at the beginning of your prompt. For example, "Photorealistic portrait of a young woman at a bustling street fair." 4. Use Reference Images: If possible, provide reference images or describe elements from existing artworks. This helps the AI understand the style and composition you’re aiming for. 5. Experiment with Length and Structure: Sometimes a short, concise prompt works best, while other times a longer, more detailed description is needed. Experiment to see what yields the best results for your specific needs. 6. Incorporate Emotions and Adjectives: Adding emotional descriptors can enhance the depth and feel of the image. For example, "a serene, misty morning in a dense forest with soft sunlight filtering through the trees." 7. Iterate and Refine: Don’t be afraid to tweak and refine your prompts. Small changes can significantly impact the final output, so keep experimenting until you get the desired result. Have you ever wondered, "How did things get so bad?" We’ve all had those moments. In hindsight, we wish we could go back in time and stop the tsunami before it crashes into the shore. But to do that, we need the right tools, the insight to understand the signs, and the accountability to act before things spiral. There’s a tool that once gave us insight into the pulse of language evolution—Wordfreq. This library tracked word frequencies across more than 40 languages, revealing which words were rising in importance and which were fading away. Wordfreq offered a glimpse into our cultural landscape, showing us our trends in politics, religion, family values, and more. It allowed us to forecast the future by analyzing the words we used. But here’s the sad truth: Wordfreq has stopped tracking word frequencies. Why? Because the internet is flooded with AI-generated content. Large language models like ChatGPT don’t generate words with emotional depth or personal context. They select the next likely word in a sequence, creating content that is often stripped of nuance and meaning. AI is creating a permanent underclass of engineers. There’s a lot of talk about AI taking over software engineering jobs, but that’s not exactly what's happening. A recent study found that AI coding tools like GitHub Copilot are making software engineers more productive, with an average increase of 26% in completed tasks. This boost is more pronounced among junior engineers, who show higher adoption rates and significantly greater productivity gains compared to their senior counterparts. Here’s the math: juniors are producing code faster than ever, but the study shows that senior engineers aren’t experiencing the same level of productivity boost. This imbalance can lead to a bottleneck where code is produced faster than it can be reviewed and integrated. Imagine a situation where juniors increase their output by 50%, but seniors only improve their review capacity by 25% because they have to double check AI generated code. Assuming that Senior engineers review all the work done by Jr. Engineers, then the result is a bottleneck—code piles up waiting for review, slowing down the workflow or forcing code through without proper checks. Neither option is ideal. This dynamic creates a real problem. Juniors are leaning heavily on AI to produce more code, but they're not developing the deeper skills needed to advance into senior roles. Meanwhile, there aren’t enough senior engineers to handle the increased volume of code. This mismatch not only affects workflow dynamics but stalls the professional growth of junior engineers. We're looking at the rise of two distinct groups: AI Code Producers: Juniors who stay stuck as juniors because they rely on AI for most of their work and miss out on the experiences that build deeper expertise. True Seniors: A shrinking group of engineers who can review and guide the AI-generated code safely into production for the long term. So no, AI isn’t replacing software engineers. It's creating a divide. And the concerning part? We might end up with a permanent gap where one group is stuck in junior roles with high output but limited growth, while the other group becomes rarer and more overwhelmed with the responsibility of maintaining quality. Mastering AI Image Generation: Top Prompt Engineering Tricks! Creating stunning AI-generated images is an art form in itself. With the right prompt engineering techniques, you can guide AI to produce visuals that perfectly match your vision. Here are some tips to help you craft the perfect prompts: 1. Be Specific and Descriptive: The more details you provide, the better the AI can understand your vision. Instead of "a beautiful landscape," try "a sunset over a tranquil lake surrounded by snow-capped mountains, with wildflowers in the foreground." 2. Front-Load Key Information: Start your prompt with the most important details. AI models often prioritize the beginning of the prompt, so make sure to include crucial elements early on. 3. Specify the Art Style: Whether you want a photorealistic image, a watercolor painting, or an anime-style drawing, clearly state the desired art style at the beginning of your prompt. For example, "Photorealistic portrait of a young woman at a bustling street fair." 4. Use Reference Images: If possible, provide reference images or describe elements from existing artworks. This helps the AI understand the style and composition you’re aiming for. 5. Experiment with Length and Structure: Sometimes a short, concise prompt works best, while other times a longer, more detailed description is needed. Experiment to see what yields the best results for your specific needs. 6. Incorporate Emotions and Adjectives: Adding emotional descriptors can enhance the depth and feel of the image. For example, "a serene, misty morning in a dense forest with soft sunlight filtering through the trees." 7. Iterate and Refine: Don’t be afraid to tweak and refine your prompts. Small changes can significantly impact the final output, so keep experimenting until you get the desired result. By mastering these prompt tricks, you can unlock the full potential of AI image generation and create visuals that truly stand out. Happy creating! Used video source: https://lnkd.in/ddBGBrHJ …more

We were able to ideate, create and debug within the 24 hours to create a mobile product to replace Aphasia patients' outdated AAC (Augmented Alternative Communication) devices. Using React Native with Expo , FastAPI , MongoDB , LangChain , among other technologies, was a great choice for us to learn lots while working fast. AI detection tools are fundamentally flawed because they're always playing catch-up in an asymmetric race. The incentives are heavily skewed towards the development of more sophisticated AI generation capabilities, leaving detection methods perpetually behind - much like we see in cybersecurity, where offensive capabilities often outpace defensive measures. The quest for reliable AI detection is misguided. Instead, we should focus on transparency and attestation. As AI becomes increasingly integrated into all aspects of content creation - from spell-checking to formatting and personalized delivery - the distinction between "AI-generated" and "human-written" content becomes meaningless. The way forward involves transparent disclosure of AI usage, clear provenance of training data and knowledge bases, and human attestation of final outputs. This approach aligns incentives towards truthful AI and maintains human accountability. At Blackwire Labs , we're exploring blockchain-based attestation systems to cryptographically verify content origins while protecting sensitive data. This allows for public verification without compromising privacy, crucial for fields like cybersecurity where data sensitivity is paramount. California is keeping us on our toes this week with not 1 or even 2, but ~8~ new Gen AI laws signed by Gov Newsom. These laws cover a range of issues related to generative AI: transparency, rights of actors/performers regarding use of their NIL, criminalizes deepfake unauthorized sexually explicit content, and use of deepfakes in elections to misinform. SB 942 – California AI Transparency Act (Signed 9/19) Requires widely-used generative AI systems to include provenance disclosures in the content they generate. SB 926 – Amends Section 647 of the Penal Code (Signed 9/19) Creates a new crime targeting AI-generated sexually explicit deepfake content. SB 981 – An act to add Chapter 22.7 (commencing with Section 22670) to Division 8 of the Business and Professions Code, relating to social media platforms (Signed 9/19) Requires social media platforms to establish a mechanism for users to report sexually explicit deepfakes of themselves. AB 1836 – An act to amend Section 3344.1 of the Civil Code, relating to intellectual property (Signed 9/17) Prohibits commercial use of digital replicas of deceased performers in films, TV shows, video games, audiobooks, sound recordings and more, without first obtaining the consent of those performers’ estates. AB 2602 - An act to add Section 927 to the Labor Code, relating to employment (Signed 9/17) Requires contracts to specify the use of AI-generated digital replicas of a performer’s voice or likeness, and the performer must be professionally represented in negotiating the contract. AB 2655 – Defending Democracy from Deepfake Deception Act of 2024 (Signed 9/17) Requires large online platforms to remove or label deceptive and digitally altered or created content related to elections during specified periods, and requires them to provide mechanisms to report such content. AB 2839 – An act to amend Section 35 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and to add Section 20012 to the Elections Code, relating to elections, and declaring the urgency thereof, to take effect immediately (Signed 9/17) Expands the timeframe in which a committee or other entity is prohibited from knowingly distributing an advertisement or other election material containing deceptive AI-generated or manipulated content. AB 2355 – An act to amend Sections 84504, 84504.1, 84504.2, 84504.3, 84054.4, and 84504.5 of, and to add Section 84514 to, the Government Code, relating to the Political Reform Act of 1974 (Signed 9/17) Requires that electoral advertisements using AI-generated or substantially altered content feature a disclosure that the material has been altered. My Berkeley College students and I designed our own AI policy together. This is how we approached it. (I'll include the basic policy at the end of this post) 1. We talked about what they already knew. → We started in teams and shared. → Then, we talked together. 2. We used ChatGPT. → Quite a few students never used it before. → Several students had no idea what this was. → We talked about what was happening. 3. We used Claude. → I wanted to move away from ChatGPT. → I showed them how it could create games. 4. We used Google'S NotebookLM. → I wanted to talk more about multimodal AI. → My students were thoroughly unimpressed. → We talked about voice clones (the good and the bad) 5. We talked about AI-generated images. → We did this with Dall-E, through ChatGPT. 6. We played Leon Furze 's Real vs. Fake Game → Students had to pick out AI-generated images. → They did well, and got 7/10. → We talked about AI and misinformation. 7. We brainstormed about benefits and risks. → We talked about using AI for brainstorming and for getting past the blank page. → We talked about the loss of voice, the unethical practices used in training, the impact on the environment. If students had a question, I answered it to the best of my knowledge. We were as holistic as possible. ----------------------- Then, we created a policy. Here is what my students wanted. 1️⃣ Full Transparency → They'll tell me when and how they use it. → I'll tell them when I use it. 2️⃣ AI Scale → They thought Leon Furze 's scale was fair. → Parts of an assignment get a number from 1-5. → 1 = No AI → 5 = Full-On AI → Most activities will be in the middle. 3️⃣ AI is to be used carefully and only for specific purposes that help us learn. → It is not to be used lightly. → It hurts our environment and can hurt our voices. → We need to use it carefully or not at all. → We can use it for brainstorming, outlining, and feedback. → But we are not allowed to use it to write. For example, "a serene, misty morning in a dense forest with soft sunlight filtering through the trees." 7. Iterate and Refine: Don’t be afraid to tweak and refine your prompts. AI is creating a permanent underclass of engineers. There’s a lot of talk about AI taking over software engineering jobs, but that’s not exactly what's happening. A recent study found that AI coding tools like GitHub Copilot are making software engineers more productive, with an average increase of 26% in completed tasks. This boost is more pronounced among junior engineers, who show higher adoption rates and significantly greater productivity gains compared to their senior counterparts. Here’s the math: juniors are producing code faster than ever, but the study shows that senior engineers aren’t experiencing the same level of productivity boost. This imbalance can lead to a bottleneck where code is produced faster than it can be reviewed and integrated. Imagine a situation where juniors increase their output by 50%, but seniors only improve their review capacity by 25% because they have to double check AI generated code. Assuming that Senior engineers review all the work done by Jr. Engineers, then the result is a bottleneck—code piles up waiting for review, slowing down the workflow or forcing code through without proper checks. Neither option is ideal. This dynamic creates a real problem. Juniors are leaning heavily on AI to produce more code, but they're not developing the deeper skills needed to advance into senior roles. Meanwhile, there aren’t enough senior engineers to handle the increased volume of code. This mismatch not only affects workflow dynamics but stalls the professional growth of junior engineers. We're looking at the rise of two distinct groups: AI Code Producers: Juniors who stay stuck as juniors because they rely on AI for most of their work and miss out on the experiences that build deeper expertise. True Seniors: A shrinking group of engineers who can review and guide the AI-generated code safely into production for the long term. So no, AI isn’t replacing software engineers. It's creating a divide. And the concerning part? We might end up with a permanent gap where one group is stuck in junior roles with high output but limited growth, while the other group becomes rarer and more overwhelmed with the responsibility of maintaining quality. AI detection tools are fundamentally flawed because they're always playing catch-up in an asymmetric race. The incentives are heavily skewed towards the development of more sophisticated AI generation capabilities, leaving detection methods perpetually behind - much like we see in cybersecurity, where offensive capabilities often outpace defensive measures. The quest for reliable AI detection is misguided. Instead, we should focus on transparency and attestation. As AI becomes increasingly integrated into all aspects of content creation - from spell-checking to formatting and personalized delivery - the distinction between "AI-generated" and "human-written" content becomes meaningless. The way forward involves transparent disclosure of AI usage, clear provenance of training data and knowledge bases, and human attestation of final outputs. This approach aligns incentives towards truthful AI and maintains human accountability. At Blackwire Labs , we're exploring blockchain-based attestation systems to cryptographically verify content origins while protecting sensitive data. This allows for public verification without compromising privacy, crucial for fields like cybersecurity where data sensitivity is paramount. CC and AI Ever since I first discovered Creative Commons during my formative years at McGill University – Faculty of Law , I’ve been captured by its simplicity and massive impact. Like the Wikimedia Foundation , the organization behind Wikipedia, the Free Encyclopedia , Creative Commons has had a massively outsized and positive effect on human knowledge and particularly creativity and intellectual property. I want to highlight Creative Commons’ recent work on artificial intelligence for creators. It charts a potential path forward that protects creators while balancing their rights with the benefits of using creative content for AI training. In the words of CC: “For over two decades we have stewarded the legal infrastructure that enables open sharing on the web. We now have an opportunity to reimagine sharing and creativity in this new age. It is time to build new infrastructure that supports better sharing with generative AI.” [...] “Generative AI presents an amazing opportunity to be a transformative tool that supports creators — both individuals and organizations — provides new avenues for creation, facilitates better sharing, enables more people to become creators, and benefits the commons of knowledge, information, and creativity for all. But there are serious concerns, such as issues around author recognition and fair compensation for creators (and the labor market for artistic work in general), the potential flood of AI-generated works on the commons making it difficult to find relevant and trustworthy information, and the disempowering effect of the privatization and enclosure of AI services and outputs, to name a few. For many creators, these and other issues may be a reason not to share their works at all under any terms, not just via CC licensing. CC wants AI to augment and support commons, not detract from it, and we want to see solutions to these concerns to avoid AI turning creators away from contributing to the commons altogether.” CC’s most recent work on GenAI has proposed the idea of Preference Sharing: “In these uncertain times, one thing is clear: there is an urgent need to develop new, nuanced approaches to digital sharing. This is Creative Commons’ speciality and we’re ready to take on this challenge by exploring a possible intervention in the AI space: preference signals.” See also their “seven principles for regulating generative AI models in order to protect the interests of creators, people building on the commons (including through AI), and society’s interests in the sustainability of the commons” linked in the comments. California is keeping us on our toes this week with not 1 or even 2, but ~8~ new Gen AI laws signed by Gov Newsom. These laws cover a range of issues related to generative AI: transparency, rights of actors/performers regarding use of their NIL, criminalizes deepfake unauthorized sexually explicit content, and use of deepfakes in elections to misinform. SB 942 – California AI Transparency Act (Signed 9/19) Requires widely-used generative AI systems to include provenance disclosures in the content they generate. SB 926 – Amends Section 647 of the Penal Code (Signed 9/19) Creates a new crime targeting AI-generated sexually explicit deepfake content. SB 981 – An act to add Chapter 22.7 (commencing with Section 22670) to Division 8 of the Business and Professions Code, relating to social media platforms (Signed 9/19) Requires social media platforms to establish a mechanism for users to report sexually explicit deepfakes of themselves. AB 1836 – An act to amend Section 3344.1 of the Civil Code, relating to intellectual property (Signed 9/17) Prohibits commercial use of digital replicas of deceased performers in films, TV shows, video games, audiobooks, sound recordings and more, without first obtaining the consent of those performers’ estates. AB 2602 - An act to add Section 927 to the Labor Code, relating to employment (Signed 9/17) Requires contracts to specify the use of AI-generated digital replicas of a performer’s voice or likeness, and the performer must be professionally represented in negotiating the contract. AB 2655 – Defending Democracy from Deepfake Deception Act of 2024 (Signed 9/17) Requires large online platforms to remove or label deceptive and digitally altered or created content related to elections during specified periods, and requires them to provide mechanisms to report such content. AB 2839 – An act to amend Section 35 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and to add Section 20012 to the Elections Code, relating to elections, and declaring the urgency thereof, to take effect immediately (Signed 9/17) Expands the timeframe in which a committee or other entity is prohibited from knowingly distributing an advertisement or other election material containing deceptive AI-generated or manipulated content. AB 2355 – An act to amend Sections 84504, 84504.1, 84504.2, 84504.3, 84054.4, and 84504.5 of, and to add Section 84514 to, the Government Code, relating to the Political Reform Act of 1974 (Signed 9/17) Requires that electoral advertisements using AI-generated or substantially altered content feature a disclosure that the material has been altered. I have witnessed this question being asked across multiple interviews, and the question might seem confusing, but the answer is too naive in itself. Let's see why! One group of people will say that they mean the opposite because of the 'in' in 'inflammable'. Which is wrong, as the word for something that is not flammable is non-flammable. It's similar to valuable and invaluable and not like complete and incomplete, to give an example. The second group of individuals, which also includes AI-generated answers, claims that something that needs a flame to be ignited is 'flammable', while certain unstable chemicals that can spontaneously ignite in the absence of an ignition source are 'inflammable'. This then means that all pyrophoric chemicals are 'inflammable'? No. They both mean the same damn thing! Something that is "capable of being easily ignited and of burning quickly" is flammable or inflammable. Then why do we need two different words? We get inflammable from the Latin verb inflammare, which combines flammare ("to catch fire") with a Latin prefix in- (more commonly seen as en- in English, as in encourage), meaning "to cause to be." This in- shows up occasionally in English words, such as indent and indebted, and it showed up in inflammable in the early 1600s. All was fine with this situation until 1813, when a scholar translating a Latin text coined the English word flammable from the Latin flammare. Now we had a problem: two words that look like antonyms but are actually synonyms. There has been confusion between the two words ever since. Preparing for GATE or Chemical Engineering Interviews? AI detection tools are fundamentally flawed because they're always playing catch-up in an asymmetric race. The incentives are heavily skewed towards the development of more sophisticated AI generation capabilities, leaving detection methods perpetually behind - much like we see in cybersecurity, where offensive capabilities often outpace defensive measures. The quest for reliable AI detection is misguided. Instead, we should focus on transparency and attestation. As AI becomes increasingly integrated into all aspects of content creation - from spell-checking to formatting and personalized delivery - the distinction between "AI-generated" and "human-written" content becomes meaningless. The way forward involves transparent disclosure of AI usage, clear provenance of training data and knowledge bases, and human attestation of final outputs. This approach aligns incentives towards truthful AI and maintains human accountability. At Blackwire Labs , we're exploring blockchain-based attestation systems to cryptographically verify content origins while protecting sensitive data. This allows for public verification without compromising privacy, crucial for fields like cybersecurity where data sensitivity is paramount. AI detection tools are fundamentally flawed because they're always playing catch-up in an asymmetric race. The incentives are heavily skewed towards the development of more sophisticated AI generation capabilities, leaving detection methods perpetually behind - much like we see in cybersecurity, where offensive capabilities often outpace defensive measures. The quest for reliable AI detection is misguided. Instead, we should focus on transparency and attestation. As AI becomes increasingly integrated into all aspects of content creation - from spell-checking to formatting and personalized delivery - the distinction between "AI-generated" and "human-written" content becomes meaningless. The way forward involves transparent disclosure of AI usage, clear provenance of training data and knowledge bases, and human attestation of final outputs. This approach aligns incentives towards truthful AI and maintains human accountability. At   Blackwire Labs , we're exploring blockchain-based attestation systems to cryptographically verify content origins while protecting sensitive data. This allows for public verification without compromising privacy, crucial for fields like cybersecurity where data sensitivity is paramount.
